sedentary

SED-un-tair-ee -- Latin sedere, 'to sit': a sedentary life is a sitting life. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sedentary is involving much sitting and little physical activity.

Worried about his sedentary desk job, Omar started biking to the office twice a week.

Example

A software tester's smartwatch buzzes at 4 p.m. with a gentle reminder of just how sedentary his day has been: in seven hours, he has taken exactly 212 steps, all of them between his desk and the coffee machine.

A routine spent almost entirely sitting still is what sedentary measures. Unlike 'lazy,' which judges someone's character, sedentary neutrally describes a lack of physical movement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

desk-bound: Desk-bound describes someone kept at a desk for long hours by the nature of the work. It is one common way a life turns sedentary -- but a sedentary routine can be built around a couch or a checkout counter just as easily.

sluggish: Sluggish means moving slowly for lack of energy -- a drained, heavy slowness. Sedentary says nothing about energy: a sedentary programmer can be sharp and quick all day, just seated. Sluggish describes how you move; sedentary, how little you move.

stationary: Stationary means not moving from a spot right now -- a stationary car at a red light, a guard standing at his post. Sedentary describes a long-term pattern of sitting, not a single moment: a sedentary job, a sedentary winter.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

active: physically energetic and moving often

mobile: moving or able to move about easily

Where it sits · how little movement remains

inactive → sedentary → immobile

inactive vs. sedentary: Inactive is the milder, more general word here -- an inactive person just is not moving much lately, while sedentary makes a firmer claim: a whole routine built around sitting, day after day.

immobile vs. sedentary: Immobile is more extreme than sedentary: a sedentary person still walks around, just not much, while immobile means barely able to move at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — sed-: to sit (Latin (sedere))

suffix — -entary: relating to, characterized by (Latin (-arius))

Put it together: Latin sedentarius meant 'sitting' -- from sedere, 'to sit' -- so a sedentary job is literally a sitting job, the same root that gives us sediment, the material that sits at the bottom of a lake.

Use the root in a new word: sediment: Farmers along the Nile once planned their whole year around the river's sediment.

Root Check

Word Choice

Sedentary most often modifies 'lifestyle,' 'job,' or 'work,' describing physical inactivity -- it comments on how much a body moves, not on how hard a person works.
